Changes in population size were unable to effectively predict the level of life expectancy in these countries. In contrast, infant mortality rate was a more crucial predictive factor.

title: Data Exercise(Week4)
text:
In this section, I generate a synthetic dataset (N=1000) representing an older adult population (50+). The underlying logic includes:


Age & Depression: Strong risk factors for dementia.
Education & Physical Activity: Protective factors.
Comorbidities (Diabetes/Hypertension): Driven by Age and BMI.
BMI & Dementia: A U-shaped relationship(both underweight and obese increase risk).


# 0) Load required packages
library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.0     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.2     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.1     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(ggplot2)
# 1) Reproducibility seed
base::set.seed(1)

# 2) functions
inv_logit <- function(x) 1 / (1 + base::exp(-x))
clamp <- function(x, lower, upper) base::pmax(lower, base::pmin(x, upper))

# 3) Sample size
N <- 1000

# 4) Generate synthetic dataset
synthetic_data <- tibble::tibble(
  ID = base::sprintf("%05d", 1:N),

  # Age: 85% from truncated normal-like around 65, 15% from uniform tails
  age = {
    mix <- stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = 0.85)
    main <- clamp(stats::rnorm(n = N, mean = 65, sd = 7.5), 50, 95)
    tail <- stats::runif(n = N, min = 50, max = 95)
    base::as.integer(base::round(base::ifelse(mix == 1, main, tail)))
  },

  # Gender: ~52% female
  gender = {
    g <- stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = 0.52)
    base::factor(base::ifelse(g == 1, "Female", "Male"), levels = c("Male", "Female"))
  }
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Education (years): mean ~13 with mild cohort effect (older -> slightly fewer years)
    education_years = {
      edu_base <- stats::rnorm(n = N, mean = 13, sd = 2.7)
      edu <- clamp(edu_base - 0.03 * (age - 65), 0, 22)
      base::as.integer(base::round(edu))
    },

    # BMI: mean ~27 sd ~5, mild age pattern, clamped
    BMI = {
      bmi_base <- stats::rnorm(n = N, mean = 27, sd = 5)
      bmi_val <- clamp(bmi_base + 0.03 * (pmin(age, 70) - 50), 15, 55)
      base::round(bmi_val, 1)
    },

    # Physical activity: ordered factor influenced by education (+) and age (-)
    physical_activity = {
      latent <- 0.12 * (education_years - 12) - 0.03 * (age - 65) + stats::rnorm(n = N)
      pa <- base::cut(
        latent,
        breaks = c(-Inf, -0.4, 0.8, Inf),
        labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"),
        right = TRUE
      )
      base::factor(pa, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"), ordered = TRUE)
    },

    # Depression history: ~15–20% with links to age and physical activity
    depression_history = {
      lp <- -1.6 +
        0.012 * (age - 65) +
        0.25  * (physical_activity == "Low") -
        0.10  * (physical_activity == "High") +
        0.08  * (gender == "Female")
      stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = inv_logit(lp))
    },

    # Diabetes and hypertension: probabilities increase with age and BMI
    diabetes = {
      lp <- -2.0 + 0.035 * (age - 65) + 0.070 * (BMI - 27) + 0.15 * (gender == "Male")
      stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = inv_logit(lp))
    },

    hypertension = {
      lp <- -1.0 + 0.050 * (age - 65) + 0.040 * (BMI - 27) + 0.10 * (gender == "Male")
      stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = inv_logit(lp))
    },

    # Number of comorbidities (0,1,2) among diabetes + hypertension
    n_comorbidities = diabetes + hypertension,

    # Dementia (0/1): age & depression strong risk; edu & PA protective;
    # diabetes & hypertension risk; BMI U-shaped via quadratic term
    dementia = {
      bmi_u <- ((BMI - 27)^2) / 25
      lp <- -3.2 +
        0.075 * (age - 65) +
        0.85  * depression_history +
        (-0.08) * (education_years - 13) +
        (-0.25) * (physical_activity == "Moderate") +
        (-0.50) * (physical_activity == "High") +
        0.45  * diabetes +
        0.35  * hypertension +
        0.55  * bmi_u
      stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = inv_logit(lp))
    }
  )

    n_comorbidities = diabetes + hypertension,

    # Dementia (0/1): age & depression strong risk; edu & PA protective;
    # diabetes & hypertension risk; BMI U-shaped via quadratic term
    dementia = {
      bmi_u <- ((BMI - 27)^2) / 25
      lp <- -3.2 +
        0.075 * (age - 65) +
        0.85  * depression_history +
        (-0.08) * (education_years - 13) +
        (-0.25) * (physical_activity == "Moderate") +
        (-0.50) * (physical_activity == "High") +
        0.45  * diabetes +
        0.35  * hypertension +
        0.55  * bmi_u
      stats::rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = inv_logit(lp))
    }
  )

title: About me

Background and Training
I am a first-year PhD student in Health Services Research, with a background in statistics. My academic training has provided me with experience in quantitative methods and data analysis, and I am particularly interested in applying these tools to real-world public health and policy questions.


Research Interests
My research interests focus on public health, healthcare access, and health policy. I am especially interested in understanding how social, economic, and policy environments shape health outcomes and contribute to disparities across populations.


Data Analysis and Programming Experience
I have previously used R and Python for data analysis and visualization. While I am still building confidence and fluency in these tools, I am comfortable working with data and eager to continue improving my programming and analytical skills.


Goals for This Course
Through this course, I hope to strengthen my ability to conduct reproducible data analyses, gain more experience with modern data science tools, and further improve my proficiency in R for applied data analysis.


A Dataset I Have Been Working With
One dataset I have recently been working with is the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), a nationally representative longitudinal survey of older adults in the United States.
I have been using HRS in recent research related to dementia, which has made me particularly familiar with the structure and variables of the dataset. I find HRS especially valuable because it provides rich longitudinal information on health, socioeconomic status, and aging, allowing for applied statistical analyses that are directly relevant to public health and health policy questions.

#    (Note: in the dataset, Long Beach State is labeled as "Long Beach St.")
schools_keep <- c(
  "Louisiana Tech",
  "Long Beach St.",
  "Southern California",
  "Old Dominion"
)

# 3) Build the plotting dataset with the required columns:
#    year (1982–2018), school, seed_points (0–100)
plot_df <- raw %>%
  # Limit to the target time window and selected schools
  filter(Year >= 1982, Year <= 2018, School %in% schools_keep) %>%
  # Keep only what we need and standardize names
  transmute(
    year   = Year,
    school = School,
    seed   = as.numeric(Seed)
  ) %>%
  # Convert NCAA seed (1 is best, 16 is worst) into a 0–100 "seed points" scale
  # Higher seed_points = better seed / stronger tournament position
  mutate(seed_points = (17 - seed) / 16 * 100) %>%
  select(year, school, seed_points) %>%
  # Fill in missing years for each school (years without a tournament appearance)
  # so the line/area sits at 0, matching the look of the FiveThirtyEight figure.
  complete(
    year = 1982:2018,
    school = schools_keep,
    fill = list(seed_points = 0)
  ) %>%
  # Clean up the displayed school name and set facet order
  mutate(
    school = recode(school, "Long Beach St." = "Long Beach State"),
    school = factor(
      school,
      levels = c(
        "Louisiana Tech",
        "Long Beach State",
        "Southern California",
        "Old Dominion"

library(tidyverse)

raw <- readr::read_csv(
  here("presentation-exercise", "ncaa-womens-basketball-tournament-history.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE

# 1) Build a seed -> expected wins lookup (1982–2018)
seed_lookup <- raw %>%
  filter(Year >= 1982, Year <= 2018) %>%
  transmute(
    seed = as.numeric(Seed),
    tourney_w = as.numeric(`Tourney W`)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(seed), !is.na(tourney_w)) %>%
  group_by(seed) %>%
  summarise(exp_wins = mean(tourney_w), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(seed_points = exp_wins / exp_wins[seed == 1] * 100) %>%
  select(seed, seed_points)

# 2) Schools to plot

  filter(Year >= 1982, Year <= 2018, School %in% schools_keep) %>%

    year = Year,
    school = School,
    seed = as.numeric(Seed)
  ) %>%
  left_join(seed_lookup, by = "seed") %>%
  select(year, school, seed_points) %>%
  complete(
    year = 1982:2018,
    school = schools_keep,
    fill = list(seed_points = 0)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    school = recode(school, "Long Beach St." = "Long Beach State"),
    school = factor(
      school,
      levels = c("Louisiana Tech", "Long Beach State", "Southern California", "Old Dominion")

Write R code to create a professional summary table from the NCAA basketball dataset that includes automatically calculated statistics, bold text, conditional color formatting, a spanner header, a footnote, a caption, and inline sparklines.

# Load table formatting packages
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)

# 1) Process data: Calculate summary statistics for the top 5 schools (by total wins)
# and create a list column of their historical win trends for the sparkline.
top_schools_summary <- raw %>%
  # Filter for recent history to make sparklines legible (e.g., 2000 onwards)
  filter(Year >= 2000) %>%
  mutate(
    tourney_w = as.numeric(`Tourney W`),
    seed = as.numeric(Seed)
  ) %>%
  # Remove NA rows that might break calculations
  filter(!is.na(tourney_w), !is.na(seed)) %>%
  group_by(School) %>%
  summarize(
    Appearances = n(),
    Total_Wins = sum(tourney_w),
    Avg_Wins_per_Tourney = Total_Wins / Appearances,
    Avg_Seed = mean(seed),
    # Create a list of wins ordered by year for the sparkline
    Wins_History = list(tourney_w[order(Year)]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Keep only the top 5 schools with the most wins since 2000
  slice_max(order_by = Total_Wins, n = 5)
top_schools_summary <- top_schools_summary %>%
  mutate(School = stringr::str_replace_all(School, " ", "\u00A0"))

# 2) Build the gt table

  gt() %>%
  
  # A descriptive caption/title explaining the summary
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Modern Era Dominance: Top 5 NCAA Women's Programs**"),
    subtitle = "Tournament performance summary (2000–2018)"
  ) %>%
  tab_caption(
    "Caption: This table summarizes 2000–2018 NCAA tournament performance for the top five women’s programs by total wins. Higher W/App indicates more wins per appearance, while lower Avg Seed indicates stronger seeding; sparklines show wins by year."
  ) %>%
  # Spanning column header
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Historical Performance Metrics",
    columns = c(Total_Wins, Avg_Seed, Wins_History)
  ) %>%
  
  # Formatted text: Bold the school names
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = School)
  ) %>%
  
  # Conditional formatting: Color the average seed
  # Green is better (lower number), Red is worse (higher number)
  data_color(
    columns = Avg_Seed,
    colors = scales::col_numeric(
      palette = c("#1a9850", "#ffffbf", "#d73027"),

    Avg_Seed = "Avg Seed",
    Wins_History = "Trend"

  decimals = 1
  ) %>%

  columns = Avg_Wins_per_Tourney,
  decimals = 2

  # Add a correctly attributed footnote

  ) %>%

    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = Total_Wins)
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "W/App = Total W ÷ Apps (average wins per tournament appearance).",

  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(

    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = Avg_Seed)
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Trend = wins per year (2000–2018).",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = Wins_History)
  ) %>%
  
  # Apply a clean theme
  gt_theme_538()

Overall, the results show that model flexibility can improve performance, but proper evaluation matters. In the initial full-data fit, the random forest produced predictions closest to the observed values, while the LASSO and linear model performed almost identically. The LASSO tuning results showed that very small penalty values gave the lowest RMSE, which makes sense because a small penalty makes the LASSO behave similarly to ordinary linear regression. As the penalty increased, RMSE rose because stronger regularization shrank the coefficients too much and reduced predictive accuracy. For the random forest, better performance was observed when more features were considered at each split and smaller node sizes were allowed, suggesting that a more flexible tree structure fit the data better. However, the tuning results from apparent resampling were overly optimistic because the same data were used for both training and evaluation, which is why cross-validation is essential for reliable model assessment. The cross-validation results provided more realistic estimates of predictive performance and showed that the random forest remained the best-performing model overall.

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
This week’s Tidy Tuesday dataset comes from Te Papa Tongarewa (The Museum of New Zealand) and contains logbook entries of seabird sightings near New Zealand from 1969 to 1990. Each record corresponds to a 10-minute observation window from a ship, including the bird species observed, their behaviors, and environmental conditions such as wind speed, sea state, and season.
Question: Can environmental conditions (season, wind speed class, sea state class, and latitude) predict whether a Wandering Albatross will be observed during a given 10-minute ship survey?
We want to choose The Wandering Albatross as our target species for this exercise because it has the highest number of observation records across all surveys (11296 records when all plumage/age variants are combined).

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
Join datasets

# Join bird observations with ship-level environmental metadata,
# then attach Beaufort wind descriptions and sea state descriptions
birds_joined <- birds %>%
  left_join(ships,          by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(beaufort_scale, by = "wind_speed_class") %>%
  left_join(sea_states,     by = "sea_state_class")

# Remove bird records that have no matching ship entry
d1 <- birds_joined %>%
  filter(!is.na(date))

cat("Rows after removing unmatched records:", nrow(d1), "\n")

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
Create the binary outcome variable

# Identify all record_ids that contain at least one Wandering Albatross sighting
albatross_records <- d1 %>%
  filter(str_detect(species_common_name, "Wandering")) %>%
  distinct(record_id) %>%
  mutate(albatross_present = TRUE)

# Build a ship-level dataset: one row per survey
# Surveys not matched to albatross_records receive albatross_present = FALSE
ship_level <- ships %>%
  left_join(albatross_records, by = "record_id") %>%
  mutate(albatross_present = replace_na(albatross_present, FALSE))

Select and clean modeling variables

# Retain only the outcome and the four predictors identified as usable
# Drop all other variables, then remove any row with a missing value

model_data <- ship_level %>%
  select(
    albatross_present,   # binary outcome
    season,              # southern hemisphere season
    wind_speed_class,    # Beaufort wind scale (0-12)
    sea_state_class,     # sea state class (0-6)
    latitude             # decimal latitude (negative = southern hemisphere)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Convert outcome to factor; "present" is the positive class
    albatross_present = factor(albatross_present,
                               levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                               labels = c("absent", "present")),
    # Convert season to an unordered factor
    season            = factor(season),
    # Ensure scale variables are stored as numeric
    wind_speed_class  = as.numeric(wind_speed_class),
    sea_state_class   = as.numeric(sea_state_class)

This week we’re exploring Bird Sightings at Sea! The data this week comes from Te Papa Tongarewa, The Museum of New Zealand. It consists of log book entries of bird sightings at sea near New Zealand, from 1969 to 1990.
Thank you to David Hood for the dataset suggestion.

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
This week’s Tidy Tuesday dataset comes from Te Papa Tongarewa (The Museum of New Zealand) and contains logbook entries of seabird sightings near New Zealand from 1969 to 1990. Each record corresponds to a 10-minute observation window from a ship, including the bird species observed, their behaviors, and environmental conditions such as wind speed, sea state, and season.
Question: Can environmental conditions (season, wind speed class, sea state class, and latitude) predict whether a Wandering Albatross will be observed during a given 10-minute ship survey?
We want to choose The Wandering Albatross as our target species for this exercise because it has the highest number of observation records across all surveys (11296 records when all plumage/age variants are combined).

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
Join datasets

# Join bird observations with ship-level environmental metadata,
# then attach Beaufort wind descriptions and sea state descriptions
birds_joined <- birds %>%
  left_join(ships,          by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(beaufort_scale, by = "wind_speed_class") %>%
  left_join(sea_states,     by = "sea_state_class")

# Remove bird records that have no matching ship entry
d1 <- birds_joined %>%
  filter(!is.na(date))

cat("Rows after removing unmatched records:", nrow(d1), "\n")

Rows after removing unmatched records: 49018

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
Create the binary outcome variable

# Identify all record_ids that contain at least one Wandering Albatross sighting
albatross_records <- d1 %>%
  filter(str_detect(species_common_name, "Wandering")) %>%
  distinct(record_id) %>%
  mutate(albatross_present = TRUE)

# Build a ship-level dataset: one row per survey
# Surveys not matched to albatross_records receive albatross_present = FALSE
ship_level <- ships %>%
  left_join(albatross_records, by = "record_id") %>%
  mutate(albatross_present = replace_na(albatross_present, FALSE))

Select and clean modeling variables

# Retain only the outcome and the four predictors identified as usable
# Drop all other variables, then remove any row with a missing value

model_data <- ship_level %>%
  select(
    albatross_present,   # binary outcome
    season,              # southern hemisphere season
    wind_speed_class,    # Beaufort wind scale (0-12)
    sea_state_class,     # sea state class (0-6)
    latitude             # decimal latitude (negative = southern hemisphere)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Convert outcome to factor; "present" is the positive class
    albatross_present = factor(albatross_present,
                               levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                               labels = c("absent", "present")),
    # Convert season to an unordered factor
    season            = factor(season),
    # Ensure scale variables are stored as numeric
    wind_speed_class  = as.numeric(wind_speed_class),
    sea_state_class   = as.numeric(sea_state_class)
  ) %>%
  # Drop any row missing a predictor or the outcome
  drop_na()

# 75% training, 25% test, stratified by outcome to preserve class balance

title: Tidy Tuesday Exercise
text:
Preprocessing Recipe

# A single shared recipe is applied to all three models for a fair comparison
albatross_recipe <- recipe(albatross_present ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  # Encode the season factor as dummy variables
  # (required for logistic regression and LASSO)
  step_dummy(season) %>%
  # Normalize all numeric predictors to mean = 0, sd = 1
  # This is especially important for LASSO, which penalizes raw coefficient size
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  # Remove near-zero variance predictors that may arise after dummy encoding
  step_nzv(all_predictors())

Random Forest clearly outperformed both linear models with a mean cross-validated AUC of 0.731, compared to approximately 0.627 for Logistic Regression and LASSO. The near-identical performance of LR and LASSO suggests that regularization adds little value when only four predictors are available. All three models showed higher specificity than sensitivity , indicating that predicting true absences was easier than predicting true presences. Random Forest led on every metric, with the largest advantage in sensitivity, meaning it was notably better at detecting surveys where albatrosses were genuinely present.
